stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okafor's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Printmakers who work on Japanese kozo paper have long debated whether water-based or oil-based inks hold their color better. Kozo's long, absorbent fibers draw water-based pigment deep into the sheet, where it may be shielded from light, whereas oil-based ink tends to sit on the surface. To test this idea, conservator Mireille Okafor printed identical blocks with both inks on kozo paper and on cotton rag paper. She then exposed the prints to intense light for 500 hours and measured how much their color changed. Okafor hypothesizes that on kozo paper, water-based inks resist fading better than oil-based inks do.

Color Change after 500 Hours of Light Exposure (higher values indicate more fading)
Paper | Water-based ink | Oil-based ink
Kozo | 3.1 | 5.8
Cotton rag | 6.4 | 4.9
choices: Prints made with water-based ink showed a color change of 3.1 on kozo paper, while those on cotton rag paper showed a color change of 6.4.
On cotton rag paper, prints made with oil-based ink showed a color change of 4.9, while prints made with water-based ink showed a color change of 6.4.
On kozo paper, prints made with water-based ink showed a color change of 3.1, while prints made with oil-based ink showed a color change of 5.8.
Prints made with water-based ink showed less color change than prints made with oil-based ink on both kozo paper and cotton rag paper.
explanation: The hypothesis compares two inks, and only on kozo paper. So you need the kozo row, water-based against oil-based, with water-based fading less. Choice C gives exactly that: 3.1 is less color change than 5.8.

A.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice holds the ink fixed and changes the paper. The numbers are accurate, but the hypothesis is about water-based versus oil-based ink on kozo, not about kozo versus cotton.

B.why: You dropped the condition the claim depends on. Okafor's hypothesis applies only to kozo paper, and this choice reports only the cotton rag row, so it says nothing about her claim.

D.why: You read the table as if water-based ink won in both rows. On cotton rag paper, water-based ink faded more (6.4) than oil-based ink (4.9), so this statement is false.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus:
When gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber, one product is butyrate, a fatty acid that the cells lining the colon use as their main fuel. Different fibers are fermented by different bacterial communities, so the amount of butyrate a fiber yields may vary widely. In a four-week trial, nutrition researchers gave volunteers diets supplemented with one of three fibers and measured their daily butyrate output. The researchers define a fiber's conversion rate as the butyrate produced per gram of fiber consumed, and they hypothesize that resistant starch has a higher conversion rate than inulin does.

Fiber Intake and Butyrate Output by Diet Group
Fiber | Fiber consumed (g/day) | Butyrate produced (mmol/day)
Inulin | 20 | 30
Resistant starch | 12 | 24
Wheat bran | 25 | 20
choices: The inulin group produced 30 mmol of butyrate per day, while the resistant starch group produced 24 mmol of butyrate per day.
The resistant starch group produced 24 mmol of butyrate from 12 grams of fiber, while the inulin group produced 30 mmol from 20 grams.
The inulin group produced 30 mmol of butyrate from 20 grams of fiber, while the wheat bran group produced 20 mmol from 25 grams.
The resistant starch group consumed more fiber per day than the inulin group but produced less butyrate per day than that group.
explanation: The hypothesis is about the conversion rate the passage defines, which is butyrate divided by fiber. Resistant starch gives 24 ÷ 12 = 2.0 mmol per gram and inulin gives 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 mmol per gram. Choice B supplies both numbers you need for each fiber and shows that resistant starch's rate is higher.

A.why: You used raw totals instead of the ratio the passage defined. Inulin does produce more butyrate overall, but its group also ate more fiber. The hypothesis is about butyrate per gram, which this choice never shows.

C.why: You compared the wrong pair of groups. These figures are accurate, and they do show inulin converting better than wheat bran (1.5 vs. 0.8 per gram). The hypothesis, though, compares resistant starch with inulin.

D.why: You misread the fiber column. The resistant starch group ate less fiber (12 g) than the inulin group (20 g), not more.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Varga's conclusion?
stimulus:
Folktales passed along by word of mouth tend to lose motifs, recurring elements such as a talking animal or a forbidden door, as they move from teller to teller. Folklorist Ines Varga compared recent recordings of traditional tales with versions collected a century earlier in the same villages. Some villages had kept professional storytellers, who performed tales at seasonal festivals, and others had not. Varga concludes that the presence of professional storytellers is associated with better preservation of long tales, meaning those containing fifteen or more motifs.

Percentage of Original Motifs Retained after One Century
Tale length | Villages with professional storytellers | Villages without professional storytellers
Short (fewer than 15 motifs) | 89% | 87%
Long (15 or more motifs) | 76% | 51%
choices: In villages with professional storytellers, short tales retained 89% of their original motifs, while long tales retained 76% of them.
Short tales retained 89% of their original motifs in villages with professional storytellers and 87% in villages without them.
Long tales retained a smaller percentage of their original motifs in villages with professional storytellers than in villages without them.
Long tales retained 76% of their original motifs in villages with professional storytellers and 51% in villages without them.
explanation: Varga's conclusion applies only to long tales, and it contrasts villages with and without storytellers. You need the long-tale row read across both columns. Choice D does that and shows higher retention where storytellers were present (76% vs. 51%).

A.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice holds the village type fixed and compares short tales with long ones. Varga's claim is about whether storytellers make a difference for long tales, which requires comparing the two kinds of village.

B.why: You ignored the scope word in the conclusion. Varga is talking about long tales, and this choice reports only short tales, where the two kinds of village barely differ.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Long tales kept more of their motifs in villages with storytellers (76%) than in villages without them (51%).

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken Mehta's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Cities are usually warmer than the surrounding countryside, a pattern known as the urban heat island. One contributor is waste heat. In winter, buildings are heated indoors, that heat escapes through walls and roofs, and the escaping heat warms the city's air. The effect should be most noticeable after sunset, when solar warming no longer masks it. Climatologist Arjun Mehta therefore hypothesizes that the difference between urban and rural nighttime temperatures is greater in winter than in summer.

Average Urban-Rural Temperature Difference in One City (°C)
Season | Daytime | Nighttime
Summer | 1.2 | 3.4
Winter | 0.9 | 2.1
choices: The average urban-rural temperature difference on winter days was 0.9°C, compared with 1.2°C on summer days.
The average urban-rural temperature difference on winter nights was 2.1°C, compared with 3.4°C on summer nights.
The average urban-rural temperature difference on winter nights was 2.1°C, compared with 0.9°C on winter days.
The average urban-rural temperature difference on winter nights was greater than the difference on summer nights.
explanation: Start by writing down the direction. If Mehta is right, the nighttime difference should be larger in winter than in summer. To weaken that, you need the nighttime column to show the opposite, and it does: 2.1°C in winter against 3.4°C in summer. Choice B reports that comparison.

A.why: You ignored the condition the hypothesis depends on. Mehta's claim is limited to nighttime temperatures. The daytime column is accurate here, but it cannot weaken a claim about nights.

C.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice holds the season fixed and compares night with day. That fits the passage's point about sunset, but it doesn't test whether winter nights show a bigger difference than summer nights.

D.why: You misread the nighttime column. The winter night difference (2.1°C) is smaller than the summer night difference (3.4°C). Even if this statement were true, it would support Mehta's hypothesis rather than weaken it.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Many polymers can partly repair cracks on their own. When fractured surfaces are pressed together, polymer chains drift across the gap and tangle together again, although this process slows sharply in the cold. Materials scientists therefore embedded tiny capsules of liquid healing agent in one polymer, expecting capsules broken by a crack to release agent that bonds the surfaces. The team measured each specimen's healing efficiency, defined as its strength after repair divided by its original strength. They hypothesized that capsules raise healing efficiency at 5°C, when chain movement is limited.

Specimen Strength before and after Repair (MPa)
Specimen | Original strength | Strength after repair
With capsules, 5°C | 40 | 30
Without capsules, 5°C | 60 | 33
With capsules, 25°C | 40 | 34
Without capsules, 25°C | 60 | 51
choices: At 5°C, specimens with capsules measured 30 MPa after repair out of an original 40 MPa, while specimens without capsules measured 33 out of 60 MPa.
At 5°C, specimens without capsules measured 33 MPa after repair, while specimens with capsules measured only 30 MPa after repair.
At 25°C, specimens with capsules measured 34 MPa after repair out of an original 40 MPa, while specimens without capsules measured 51 out of 60 MPa.
Specimens with capsules measured 34 MPa after repair at 25°C, while the same kind of specimens measured only 30 MPa after repair at 5°C.
explanation: The hypothesis is about healing efficiency, which is a ratio, and only at 5°C. At that temperature, specimens with capsules recovered 30 ÷ 40 = 75% of their strength and specimens without capsules recovered 33 ÷ 60 = 55%. Choice A gives both ratios and shows that the capsules raised efficiency.

B.why: You used raw values instead of the ratio the passage defined. Specimens without capsules do end up slightly stronger, but they started much stronger. Healing efficiency depends on original strength, which this choice leaves out.

C.why: You ignored the condition the hypothesis depends on. The claim concerns 5°C. At 25°C, both kinds of specimen recover 85% of their strength, so this row doesn't bear on the hypothesis.

D.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice compares specimens with capsules at two temperatures. The hypothesis compares specimens with and without capsules at 5°C, so this choice never tests whether the capsules help.
